e.t: Adōnias, also rendered Athonias, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, with most occurrences in 1 Kings and one in 2 Chronicles. The name itself does not function as a common noun or verb, so its meaning is primarily its role as a personal designation. Its significance in any particular passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding account.

This noun means “displacement; rejection.” It names the act or result of setting something or someone aside, removing it from an accepted place or position. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 24:12, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its central idea remains clear: something is treated as no longer accepted or retained. The surrounding verse context is needed to determine precisely what is being rejected or displaced there.

This verb means “choose”: to select one person, thing, or course rather than another. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it describes an act of deliberate selection. It occurs 23 times, chiefly in Old Testament books, so its basic sense is consistent across a range of passages. The surrounding sentence determines what is being chosen, but the word itself emphasizes the decision or selection. Its clearest English rendering is “choose.”

This noun means “shame”: the disgrace, dishonor, or painful sense of humiliation associated with wrongdoing, exposure, defeat, or an unworthy condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a state or experience rather than an action. The word occurs 72 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing across historical books, Psalms, wisdom writings, and the prophets. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and whether the shame is experienced personally, brought upon someone, or recognized as a fitting consequence.

This Greek LXX noun means “apathy” or “indifference”: a lack of concern, feeling, or active interest. It describes an inward state in which a person is unmoved or does not respond with needed care. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, appearing once each in Psalms, Isaiah, Sirach, and Baruch. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central idea remains emotional or practical unconcern.

This adjective describes someone or something belonging to a foreign nation, or appearing outlandish. It marks what is unfamiliar because it comes from outside the people or setting being discussed. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:6; the available information identifies its basic meaning but does not provide the verse text for explaining its particular use there.

This Greek LXX noun means “carriage,” referring to a wheeled vehicle used to carry people or goods. It names a practical means of transportation rather than an abstract idea or action. The word appears 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including passages involving travel and the movement of people or supplies. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains a carriage or transport vehicle.

This noun means “threshold,” the entrance edge or sill at the base of a doorway. It identifies the boundary one crosses when entering or leaving a place, rather than the whole doorway or building. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 5:4. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual verse wording, but the word itself names the doorway’s threshold. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s Old Testament setting.

This LXX Greek verb means “uncover”: to remove what hides something or to bring what is concealed into view. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears 19 times across the Greek Old Testament, including Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel, showing its use for revealing what was hidden. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “without pain.” It describes someone or something not experiencing pain, or not affected by it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 14:23. Its basic meaning is clear, but the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what or whom it describes there. The word therefore points to freedom from pain rather than expressing an action or a separate spiritual quality.

This verb means “respond against”: it describes answering someone in opposition rather than simply giving a neutral reply. As a verb in the Greek Old Testament, it presents a response directed back toward another person, often with a challenging or disputing force. It occurs twice in the Greek text of Job, in Job 16:8 and Job 32:12. The surrounding verse determines whether the opposition is expressed through words, argument, or a direct answer.

This Greek LXX verb means to form something from a model or to express it. It describes bringing an idea, shape, or representation into a recognizable form. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 13:13; the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly how the action functions there.

Arbattois, also rendered Arvattis, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place named in the Greek LXX text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 5:23. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise referent cannot be identified further here; the lexical meaning is simply the name itself.

This word means “obsequiousness”—an overly eager effort to please or win approval. As a noun, it describes a kind of behavior rather than an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 31:30. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s basic sense points to pleasing behavior that may be excessive or servile rather than genuine virtue.

This adjective means “best,” describing something as superior or excellent among others. It identifies the highest quality or position rather than merely something good. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains a superlative description of what stands above the rest.

Asadia is a proper name, rendered as “Asadia” or “Asathia.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:20. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, no further meaning should be assigned beyond recognizing it as this proper name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Asoriōnain” or “Asorionen.” It identifies a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:23. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here. Its meaning is therefore the preserved name itself, with its significance determined by the surrounding passage.

This adverb means “securely” or “certainly,” describing something done with safety, reliability, or firm assurance. It can tell a reader that an action is carried out safely or that a statement is established as true and dependable. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, from Genesis through 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains confidence, security, or certainty.

This word is a noun that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Its basic sense is “wrong time”. As a noun, it identifies a time understood as wrong or unsuitable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Psalms 118:147, Isaiah 59:9, and Zephaniah 1:15. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains focused on a time that is not right.

This word is a proper name rendered “Baithman” or “Vethman.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:15. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further; the lexical evidence establishes its function as a name and preserves these two supplied renderings.

Barchaboth is a noun preserved as the name “Barchaboth.” It does not carry an expanded descriptive meaning in the available lexical definition; its role is to identify rather than describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 4:21. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what or whom the name identifies there, so its normal lexical meaning is simply the name Barchaboth.

This Greek LXX adverb means “violently” or “by force.” It describes an action carried out with force rather than gently, freely, or peacefully. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, so its normal use is focused and specific rather than broad. It tells how something is done, emphasizing forceful or violent action. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This proper noun means “Galaaditēs” or “Galaathitis,” identifying a person as a Galaadite. It functions as a personal or group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, in passages from Judges, Samuel, Kings, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The precise person identified depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself marks the person by this designation.

This Greek LXX verb means “write”: to put words or information into written form. It describes the act of recording words, whether in a document, on an object, or as part of a written account. The word occurs 264 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a common term for writing across these Scriptures. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being written and the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “have dinner” or “dine,” describing the act of eating a meal. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a meal or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Daniel. The word points to ordinary meal-taking, while the surrounding passage determines the particular circumstances or significance of that meal. Its two occurrences are Proverbs 23:1 and Daniel 11:27.

gl: way of living; mode of life
d: way of living; mode of life

e.t: This noun means “way of living; mode of life.” It refers to the pattern or manner by which someone lives, rather than to one isolated action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, all in Job, where its sense concerns a person’s established way of life. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a person’s manner or condition of living.

This word means a “notion”—an idea or conception held in the mind. As a noun, it refers to what a person thinks, considers, or understands rather than to an outward action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, across Proverbs, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding statement, but its central sense remains a mental idea or understanding.

This verb means “put in through” or “insert.” It describes the action of placing something into or through another thing. As a verb, it expresses an act rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Exodus and Numbers. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being placed and where, but its central idea remains deliberate insertion or putting through.

This adjective describes something “hard to take in hand”—something difficult to grasp, handle, or manage. It points to a matter that presents real difficulty rather than being easily controlled or dealt with. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what person, situation, or matter it describes, but the central idea remains difficulty in taking hold of or dealing with something.

This verb means “bear witness to”: to testify about someone or something, affirming what is known or observed. It describes the act of giving testimony rather than merely noticing or mentioning a matter. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:36. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains the act of bearing witness or testifying to a matter.

This Greek LXX preposition means “outside; outwardly,” describing something located beyond an inside area or directed toward the exterior. It can mark position, separation, or movement in relation to what is within. The word appears 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its basic sense is used across many kinds of statements rather than belonging to one narrow subject. The surrounding words determine whether it emphasizes location beyond something or movement outward from it.

Elkia is a personal name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra and three times in Nehemiah. The available references show its use in those books, but the surrounding verse text is not provided here, so its precise role in each passage cannot be described further.

This Greek LXX noun means a “stoppage” or “barrier”—something that blocks, obstructs, or prevents movement or progress. It names an obstructing condition rather than an action, person, or emotion. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Sirach 27:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its central sense remains an impediment that interrupts or closes a way.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “embrace”: to take someone into one's arms or hold them closely. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word appears twice in the Greek text of Proverbs, at Proverbs 6:10 and Proverbs 24:33. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains the act of embracing or holding close.

This Greek verb means “destroy utterly”—to bring something to complete ruin or eliminate it entirely. It describes decisive destruction rather than a minor loss or temporary setback. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Proverbs and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains total destruction.

This verb means to look on or have regard for someone or something. It can describe directing attention toward another person or situation, with the added sense of noticing, considering, or showing attention. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 23 times, including passages from Genesis, Psalms, and other books. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what or whom the subject looks upon.

“Pursue after” means to follow or chase someone or something with determined purpose. As a verb, it describes active movement toward what is being sought rather than mere attention or observation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Genesis and once in 3 Maccabees. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains purposeful pursuit.

ἐπίνοια refers to inward mental activity: “rumination” or “conception”—the process of turning something over in the mind or forming an idea. It is a noun, so it names this act or the resulting thought. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, most often in Wisdom literature, while also appearing in Jeremiah, Sirach, and Maccabees. The exact force in any verse depends on its surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains thoughtful consideration or an idea formed in the mind.

This adjective describes someone who is “conscientious”—careful to act responsibly and faithfully. It presents a person as attentive to what should be done rather than careless or indifferent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus and once in Micah. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains conscientious conduct. Its meaning is stated directly as “conscientious.”

Ziphaios, also given as Zifeos, is a proper name. It identifies a named individual or group in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing a general quality, action, or abstract idea. The name occurs four times in the Septuagint, all within the Old Testament: three times in 1 Samuel and once in Psalms. Its precise referent in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “courage”: the inner strength or boldness that enables someone to stand firm and act despite difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears four times, including three Old Testament occurrences and one in 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on resolute confidence rather than merely feeling cheerful or hopeful. The surrounding verse determines how this courage is expressed in each passage.

This word means “wild beast” or “beast of prey,” referring to an untamed animal, especially one understood as dangerous or predatory. It is a noun used for such creatures rather than for domesticated animals. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: once in Job and four times in 2–4 Maccabees. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a wild, potentially threatening animal.

Iadias, also rendered “Iathias,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:30. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or the significance of the reference. Its meaning is therefore its use as a personal name.

Iarach, also rendered Iarakh, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is to identify an individual. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 10:26. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual description of the person or the name’s role should be added.

This word means “priest,” naming a person who serves in the priestly role. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, where it appears 829 times in this LXX corpus. Its frequent use, especially in Leviticus, Numbers, and Chronicles, reflects the regular presence of priests in Israel’s worship and community life. The precise significance in any passage depends on its surrounding context.

Iesias is a proper name—the personal name “Iesias”—rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it identifies a person named Iesias. It occurs once in this corpus, in 1 Chronicles 24:21. Because no verse text is provided here, the name itself supplies the lexical meaning, while the surrounding passage would identify the person’s role.

Iōatham is a personal name, rendered as “Iōatham” or “Ioatham.” It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 19 times in 19 verses within the Greek Old Testament corpus, from 2 Kings 15:5 through Micah 1:1. Its precise identity in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but the word itself functions as a person’s name. The supplied lexical evidence does not provide an additional definition or meaning for the name.

This adjective describes something fresh, new in character, or innovative. It can identify what has not been used before, what has been newly made, or what presents a distinct and renewed quality. Its basic sense is broader than merely recent: the emphasis is on freshness or newness. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 42 times, showing regular use for describing things, conditions, or actions as fresh or innovative.

This verb means “invent”: to devise or originate something. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used five times, appearing once in Genesis and four times in Isaiah. Its central idea is bringing something newly devised into existence, whether referring to a human creation or to what God has brought about. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but “invent” gives the word’s basic meaning and function.

This Greek LXX verb means to “plot against”—to take part in a planned effort directed against someone. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality, so it presents opposition as something people do. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is an active plot or scheme against another. This Greek LXX noun refers to the hollow area below the ribs—the flank or side of the body. It names a specific part of the human torso rather than an emotion, action, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning remains the bodily area beneath the ribs.

Kleopatra is a proper name, referring to a woman named Kleopatra rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the name occurs three times: once in Esther and twice in 1 Maccabees. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is simply the identification of that individual; what she does or represents in any particular passage must be learned from the surrounding verse and context.

This noun refers to a piece of furniture used as a “sideboard” or “cup stand,” a place or stand for holding cups and similar vessels. It is a concrete household object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:32. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and immediate context, but its ordinary lexical sense is the furnishing itself.

This LXX noun means “head man of a village,” referring to the person who leads or presides over a village community. It is a specific title for a local village leader, rather than a general word for any man or official. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Esther 2:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word is a proper name rendered “Ladabar; Lathavar.” It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The form appears twice in the LXX corpus, both times in 2 Samuel 9, at 2 Samuel 9:4 and 9:5. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific role in those sentences cannot be explained further, but its basic lexical function is a name preserved in two closely connected references.

This word means a machine for hurling stones—a catapult. It is a noun naming a device made to throw stones at a target. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:51. The word refers to the machine itself rather than to the stones it launches, giving readers a clear name for this kind of siege equipment. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “ravage”: to damage, ruin, or lay waste to something. It describes destructive action rather than merely touching or disturbing something. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. As a verb, it tells what someone or something does—bringing severe harm to a person, place, or possession. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Manachathi, also rendered Manakhathi, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an idea or action. It identifies a named person or designation in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to say more about whom the name identifies or what role it has. It occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:6.

This Greek LXX noun means “string,” referring to a strong, cordlike strand or sinew. It is used for something that can bind, be pulled tight, or form part of the body’s connective strength. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages in Genesis, Judges, Job, Ezekiel, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage speaks of a physical cord, a bodily sinew, or something compared with one.

Νηριγελ is a proper name, rendered as “Nērigel” or “Niriyel.” It identifies a particular person or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:30. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further, but the word itself functions as a personal designation. The two supplied forms are variant renderings of the same name, not separate meanings.

Nomee is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:20. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding genealogy, its specific identity and significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. The name itself is presented as “Nomee,” without an additional definition or ordinary descriptive meaning.

This verb means “make fewer; make lesser,” describing an action that reduces the number, amount, or extent of something. It presents reduction as something done, rather than merely describing something as small. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 48:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains bringing something down in quantity or degree.

gl: observe birds; watch birds for omens
d: observe birds; watch birds for omens

e.t: This verb means to observe birds or watch them for omens. It describes using birds as signs to seek guidance or predict what may happen, rather than simply noticing birds in nature. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 19:26. The word’s central sense is therefore connected with divination through observing birds. The surrounding verse provides the specific command and context in which this practice is mentioned.

This word is the name “Waw,” also given as “Ouau.” It functions as a noun rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:41. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its exact role in that passage cannot be stated more specifically. Its central meaning is the designation “Waw” (also “Ouau”) as used in that Greek Old Testament passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “crag,” referring to a prominent mass or face of rock. It names a physical rocky feature rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, with occurrences spread across Exodus, Job, Proverbs, Daniel, Nahum, and Zechariah. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a crag or rocky height.

Paralogismos refers to false reasoning or deception: thinking or presenting something in a misleading way rather than according to truth. It is a noun, so it names the deceptive reasoning or act of misleading itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, making it an uncommon word in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains reasoning or conduct that misleads.

This verb means to spring beyond something or to transgress—to go past a boundary or step beyond what is permitted. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:1. The surrounding verse would be needed to show whether the emphasis is on physically moving beyond something or on crossing a stated limit.

In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, this verb means “insert against; interpose.” It describes placing something or someone between others, or setting a person or group in position against another. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 179 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, with especially frequent use in Numbers and 1 Maccabees. The exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being placed and what it stands between.

This Greek LXX noun means “feast,” referring to a meal or celebration prepared for people to share. It names the gathering or occasion itself rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:31. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise force in that occurrence must be understood from the passage around it. Its central idea remains a communal feast or celebratory meal.

This Greek LXX word means “rich,” describing someone or something possessing abundance or material prosperity. It can function as an adjective, identifying a person, place, or thing as wealthy, and it can also function as a noun for a rich person. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament, across books including Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as abundant or prosperous.

This word means “near” or “neighbor.” It can describe something that is close by, indicate nearness, or refer to another person as a neighbor. Thus, its basic idea is closeness—either in location or in relation to someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 202 times, showing regular use for both physical nearness and the people regarded as near to one another. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “very careful.” It describes acting or attending with exceptional care rather than casually or carelessly. As a verb, it expresses careful action or treatment in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Psalms. The surrounding verse determines what is being handled carefully, but the word itself emphasizes thorough attentiveness.

gl: blow up; swell out by blowing
d: blow up; swell out by blowing

e.t: This verb describes something being blown up or swelling outward through blowing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Numbers 5. The word focuses on physical expansion: something puffs up or bulges as air causes it to rise. Its precise force in each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense is clear: to blow up or swell out by blowing.

This Greek LXX verb means “hand forth” or “make ready.” It describes presenting, appointing, or preparing someone or something for a purpose, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is established across more than one setting without being a frequently repeated word. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on handing someone forward or making something ready.

This adjective means “spotted,” describing an animal or other thing marked with distinct spots. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in six verses in Genesis, where it identifies animals by the visible pattern of their coloring. Its basic function is descriptive: it tells the reader what something looks like rather than naming an action or expressing an abstract idea. The word’s precise significance in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Rapha, also rendered Rhafa, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in passages from 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it is safest to understand Rapha as the personal or family name identified by the passage, without assigning it an additional meaning. Its precise reference in each occurrence must be determined from the surrounding context.

Raphōn, also rendered Rhafon, is a proper name rather than a common word with a broader everyday meaning. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament-related corpus, but the available information does not specify which. The name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:37. Its precise identity and significance must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself.

Romma is a proper name, also given as “Rhomma.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 25:44. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be identified from the name alone. The word itself functions as a name, not as a description with a broader ordinary meaning.

This word is a proper name for a place called “Sour” or “Sur.” It functions as a name rather than a description of taste or character. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 10 verses, including references in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and later historical books. The available references show that it identifies a geographic location, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular significance in any one passage.

This word means “sparrow,” the name of a bird. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, for that bird rather than as a broad term for birds in general. It occurs eight times in eight verses in this corpus, appearing in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “sprout together”: it describes plants or growth emerging as one joined or interwoven growth. It is a concrete word connected with vegetation and the way growth develops from the earth. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:13. The word’s central idea is combined sprouting rather than separate growth, though the exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This adverb means “sensibly”: it describes acting, thinking, or speaking with sound judgment and self-control rather than recklessly or foolishly. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Wisdom 9:11. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical sense, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain precisely what action or attitude it modifies there. The word therefore points to a sensible, well-judged manner of doing something.

Talman is a personal name identifying a particular person, not a word describing an action, quality, or general idea. Within the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:17. The name itself tells us who is being identified, but it does not by itself explain that person’s role or significance. Those details must come from the surrounding biblical passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a graveyard or to burial—the place where a dead person is laid, or the act of laying the dead to rest. It is used in passages concerning burial and the resting place of the dead, including references in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Job, and Ecclesiastes. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, covering both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact emphasis—place or act—depends on how it functions in the surrounding sentence.

This word means a frying pan or saucepan, a noun naming a cooking vessel used for preparing food. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it refers to an ordinary kitchen utensil rather than an abstract idea or action. It occurs 13 times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Samuel, Chronicles, and the Maccabean books. Its exact use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX preposition means “over” or “for,” expressing a position above something or a connection made on behalf of someone or something. Its precise sense depends on the surrounding sentence, but these two ideas provide its ordinary range. It occurs 396 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a well-established preposition used across many kinds of passages. The word appears from Genesis through Song of Songs, including poetic and historical books.

This adjective describes something as excellent—surpassing what is ordinary or standing out in quality. It expresses the idea of being notably superior or remarkable. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:31, and is rendered “excellent.” Because the word is an adjective, it qualifies a person, thing, or appearance rather than naming an action. Its precise force in Daniel 2:31 is best understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means a “play-actor,” a person who performs or presents a role. It describes someone associated with acting rather than speaking of an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, at Job 34:30 and Job 36:13. Those references identify its limited usage in this corpus, while the central meaning remains a person who acts out a part.

This is a proper name, rendered “Phadaias” or “Fatheas.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in 1 Chronicles 3:18 and once in Nehemiah 8:4. The available information gives the name’s identification but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so those references do not establish additional meaning beyond its use as a personal name.

This Greek LXX noun describes someone who is contemptuous—showing scorn or treating others with disdain. Its central idea is an attitude of looking down on others rather than honoring them. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Zephaniah 2:15. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage would be needed to explain exactly whom the word describes in that occurrence.

Philippos, also rendered Filippos, is a proper name used for a person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs eleven times, all in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is identification rather than a description of character, action, or spiritual quality. The name appears in historical narratives involving different people, so the surrounding passage is needed to determine which Philippos is intended in a particular verse.

This Greek LXX adverb means “kindly.” It describes how someone speaks or acts when showing friendly goodwill, gentleness, or considerate treatment. As an adverb, it modifies an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 9:21; its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to levying tribute—the act of collecting required payments or goods from people. It identifies a tribute-levier or the role associated with demanding such payment, rather than describing tribute itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Ezra and Job. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the collection or imposition of tribute.

This word means “bridle,” the piece used to guide or control a horse. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in 2 Kings, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and Zechariah. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning remains a bridle used for directing an animal.

Chelkia, also written Khelkia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals mentioned four times: twice in 2 Kings and once each in 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles. The name appears in 2 Kings 22:12, 2 Kings 23:4, 1 Chronicles 9:11, and 2 Chronicles 34:20. Its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and person being discussed.

This Greek LXX noun means “egg,” referring to the oval object produced by a bird. It is a concrete everyday word rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times in two verses: twice in Deuteronomy 22:6 and once in Isaiah 59:5. These references reflect its ordinary lexical sense, while the precise force of each passage comes from its surrounding verse and context.
